summary: Defines a CMS content type for compressed data. Compression before signing or encryption removes redundancy and reduces message size. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary:
RFC 3274 lets a CMS message carry compressed content. CMS is the container format used for signed and encrypted mail, so a message can be squeezed before it is signed or encrypted, and every later step has less data to work through.

The compressed content is held in a small structure with three fields: a version number, the identifier of the compression algorithm, and the content itself. ZLIB is the only algorithm required, and an implementation should announce that it can handle compressed content.

questions: which compression algorithm does cms use
what is the compresseddata content type
subtitle: A CMS content type that carries compressed data, so later steps have less to process.

tldr.problem: Signed and encrypted mail carries more data than it needs to when the content repeats itself, and every later step has to process all of it. Compressing at the MIME or TLS level does not solve that, because the CMS layer still sees the uncompressed content.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3274 adds a CompressedData content type to CMS. It is a three-field ASN.1 structure holding a version, a compression algorithm identifier and the encapsulated content, and it uses the ZLIB compression format.
tldr.outcome: The document is a Standards Track specification from June 2002 with no successor. It notes that compressing before encryption can help, but that mixing untrusted data with sensitive data before compression can leak information through the compression ratio.

today: RFC 3274 is a Standards Track specification published in June 2002. It has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the definition of the CompressedData content type for CMS and of the requirement to support ZLIB.

sections.title: Why Compress a CMS Message
sections.content:
Compressing data before transmission brings a number of advantages. It removes redundancy that could help an attacker, it speeds up processing by reducing the amount of data that later steps, such as signing or encryption, have to process, and it reduces the overall message size.

There have been proposals for adding compression at other levels, for example at the MIME or SSL level, but those do not address compression of CMS content unless the compression is supplied by an external means, such as by intermixing MIME and CMS. This document describes a compressed data content type for CMS. It is implemented as a new ContentInfo type and is an extension to the types currently defined in CMS.

CMS implementations should include support for the CompressedData content type. The format of the messages is described in ASN.1.
sections.plainLanguage: Compressing before signing or encrypting means less data for the later steps to chew through, and it removes repetition from the message. Compressing higher up, at the MIME or TLS layer, does not achieve this because the CMS layer would still see the original content.

sections.title: The CompressedData Structure
sections.content:
The compressed data content type consists of content of any type, compressed using a specified algorithm. The object identifier that identifies it is id-ct-compressedData, which is { iso(1) member-body(2) us(840) rsadsi(113549) pkcs(1) pkcs-9(9) smime(16) ct(1) 9 }.

The content type has the ASN.1 type CompressedData, a sequence of three fields. The version is the syntax version number and must be 0. The compressionAlgorithm is a compression algorithm identifier. The encapContentInfo is the content which is compressed, of the EncapsulatedContentInfo type defined in CMS.

Implementations should use the SMIMECapabilities attribute to indicate their ability to process compressed content types. A compression SMIMECapability consists of the AlgorithmIdentifier for the supported compression algorithm, which for the algorithm in this document is id-alg-zlibCompression. The use of compression may instead be handled by prior arrangement, for example as part of an interoperability profile.

The SMIMECapability sequence representing the ability to process content compressed with the algorithm identified by id-alg-zlibCompression must be DER-encoded as the hexadecimal string 30 0D 06 0B 2A 86 48 86 F7 0D 01 09 10 03 08.
sections.plainLanguage: The compressed content sits in a structure with three fields: a version number that must be 0, the name of the compression algorithm, and the content itself. An implementation says it can handle compressed content by putting the algorithm's identifier in the SMIMECapabilities attribute of the message.

sections.title: The ZLIB Compression Algorithm
sections.content:
CMS implementations that support the CompressedData content type must include support for the ZLIB compression algorithm, which has a freely available, portable and efficient reference implementation. The object identifier that identifies ZLIB is id-alg-zlibCompress, which is { iso(1) member-body(2) us(840) rsadsi(113549) pkcs(1) pkcs-9(9) smime(16) alg(3) 8 }.

This algorithm has no parameters. The parameters field should be encoded as omitted, but may be encoded as NULL.
sections.plainLanguage: ZLIB is the one algorithm the specification insists on, so that any two implementations can read each other's messages. It takes no parameters, and the field that would hold them is normally left out.

sections.title: Two Encodings for the Parameters Field
sections.content:
ZLIB allows for a number of compression levels, ranging from good but slow compression to less good but fast compression. The compression level is always compatible with the decompression algorithm, so there is no need to specify the compression level as an algorithm parameter.

There are two possible encodings for the ZLIB null parameters field. The cause is a change in the syntax of the AlgorithmIdentifier structure: when the 1988 syntax was translated into the 1997 syntax, the OPTIONAL associated with the parameters got lost. It was recovered later through a defect report, but by then everyone thought that algorithm parameters were mandatory. Some implementations therefore encode null parameters as an ASN.1 NULL element and some omit them entirely.

Although the correct encoding is to omit the parameters field, implementations may encounter encodings that use an ASN.1 NULL element for the parameters.
sections.plainLanguage:
The compression level does not need to be recorded, because whatever level was used, the same decompressor can read it.

One field is a genuine trap. An old change to the ASN.1 syntax briefly hid the fact that algorithm parameters were optional, and implementations split into two camps: some leave the field out and some write an empty value. A reader has to accept both.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document is not concerned with security, except for the fact that compressing data before encryption can enhance the security provided by other processing steps, by reducing the quantity of known plaintext available to an attacker.

Implementations should be aware of possible security threats of combining security sensitive material with possibly untrusted data before the compression and encryption. This is because information about the sensitive data may be inferred from knowing the untrusted data and the compression ratio.
sections.plainLanguage: Compression helps security in one way: there is less known plaintext for an attacker to work with. It hurts in another. If untrusted data is compressed together with sensitive data, the size of the result can reveal something about the sensitive part, because the compression ratio changes depending on what was mixed in.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The CompressedData content type and the compression algorithms are identified by object identifiers. The identifiers were assigned from an arc contributed to the S/MIME Working Group by RSA Security. Should additional compression algorithms be introduced, the advocates for such algorithms are expected to assign the necessary object identifiers from their own arcs. No action by the IANA is necessary for this document or any anticipated updates.
sections.plainLanguage: The object identifiers come from a range that RSA Security gave to the S/MIME working group. Any future compression algorithm would use an identifier from the range of whoever proposes it, so the IANA has nothing further to do here.
